questions.question: Which norm appears for normal convergence?
options: The Euclidean norm of an input vector
The taxicab norm of the graph
The uniform norm $\|f_n\|_\infty$
The absolute value of the index $n$

questions.question: Why does normal convergence express strong control over the function terms?
options: Because each value $f_n(x)$ must be equal to zero.
Because the domain $X$ must have only one point.
Because it ignores the sizes of the terms and only studies their signs.
Because the worst-case sizes $\|f_n\|_\infty$ are summable.

questions.question: Suppose $\|f_n\|_\infty\leq 3^{-n}$ for every $n$. Which conclusion follows from the definition?
options: $\sum f_n(x)$ is normally divergent.
Only pointwise convergence can be concluded.
$\sum f_n(x)$ is normally convergent.
The functions are necessarily all zero.

questions.question: If a series of functions is normally convergent, which conclusion is immediately supported?
options: It cannot converge uniformly.
It has no absolute convergence property.
It converges pointwise.
Each $f_n$ must be continuous.

questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects uniform absolute convergence?
options: Uniform absolute convergence does not necessarily imply normal convergence.
Uniform absolute convergence always implies normal convergence.
Normal convergence and pointwise convergence are equivalent.
Normal convergence fails whenever the domain is infinite.

questions.question: Why is boundedness of the terms relevant for normal convergence?
options: Because $\|f_n\|_\infty$ is used for each term.
Because bounded functions cannot form infinite series.
Because boundedness alone already implies normal convergence.
Because the domain must be a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Consider terms with $\|f_n\|_\infty = \frac{1}{n^{2}}$. Which conclusion follows?
options: The series is not pointwise convergent.
The series is uniformly convergent but not normally convergent.
The series is normally convergent.
No conclusion can be drawn because $\frac{1}{n^{2}}$ is positive.

questions.question: For $n\ge1$, define $f_n\colon\mathbb{N}^+\to\mathbb{R}$ by $f_n(x)=1/n$ when $x=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Why does $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n$ fail to converge normally?
options: Because $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty = \sum \frac{1}{n}$ diverges.
Because $f_n(x)$ is never zero.
Because the pointwise values are all negative.
Because each $f_n$ is unbounded.

questions.question: When is $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)$ normally convergent?
options: When $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)$ is pointwise divergent.
When $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty \lt +\infty$.
When each $f_n$ is unbounded.
When the first function $f_1$ is zero.

questions.question: Which implication chain starts from normal convergence?
options: Normal convergence implies pointwise divergence.
Normal convergence implies discontinuity.
Normal convergence implies that the terms are all unbounded.
Normal convergence implies uniform absolute convergence.

questions.question: If $\|f_n\|_\infty\le 2^{-n}$ for all $n$, what follows?
options: $\sum f_n$ is not normally convergent.
The functions are unbounded.
$\sum f_n$ converges pointwise but not uniformly.
$\sum f_n$ is normally convergent.

questions.question: If $\sum \|f_n\|_\infty$ converges, which convergence of $\sum f_n(x)$ follows directly?
options: Pointwise divergence
Failure of absolute convergence
Uniform convergence
Nonexistence of all pointwise limits

questions.question: If $\|f_n\|_\infty=1/n^2$, what can be concluded about $\sum f_n$?
options: It is not normally convergent because $1/n^2$ is positive.
It is pointwise divergent everywhere.
It cannot be compared with a numerical series.
It is normally convergent.

questions.question: Suppose $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty$ is the harmonic series. What does this show about normal convergence?
options: Normal convergence holds because the terms go to zero.
Uniform absolute convergence automatically fails.
Normal convergence holds because each term is bounded.
Normal convergence fails.
